summary: Introduces the Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol, which gives routers a two-way, event-driven channel to their radio modems. Through it, the router learns changing link characteristics such as speed and state so it can make better routing decisions.

plainLanguage.summary: DLEP is a conversation between a router and the modem attached to it. The modem tells the router which far-end nodes can be reached and what the link to each one is worth right now: how fast, how slow in delay, how good. When something changes, the modem says so at once, and the router can change its routing decisions immediately.

questions: how routers learn radio link quality
how do routers learn radio link quality
subtitle: How a router and its radio or satellite modem keep each other posted on changing link speed, delay and reachability.

tldr.problem: A router that reaches the network through a radio or satellite modem needs timely knowledge of the link: its speed, its delay, and whether the far end is there at all. Manual configuration cannot keep up, and routing protocols that rely on interface state and timers cannot see a link that comes and goes.
tldr.mechanism: DLEP opens a session between the router and its modem over a local TCP connection and exchanges typed messages over it. The modem reports destinations appearing and disappearing and the metrics of the link to each one, and the router may ask for a different data rate or latency.
tldr.outcome: The router can maintain an accurate picture of the link and act on changes as they happen, instead of waiting for timers to expire. The document is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 8175 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2017, and it has not been obsoleted. It defines the Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol, a session protocol between a router and its modem, and registers the port 854 and the link-local multicast addresses used for discovery.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
There exists today a collection of modem devices that control links of variable data rate and quality. Examples include line-of-sight terrestrial radios, satellite terminals, and broadband modems. Fluctuations in speed and quality of these links can occur due to configuration, or on a moment-to-moment basis due to physical phenomena like multipath interference, obstructions, and rain fade. Link quality and data rate can also vary with respect to individual destinations on a link and with the type of traffic being sent. In an IEEE 802.11 access point serving two associated laptops, the answer to the question of what the data rate on the link is depends on which laptop is meant and what kind of traffic is being sent. The closer laptop may have a data rate of 54 Mbps for unicast traffic, while the other, being relatively far away or obstructed, can simultaneously have a data rate of only 32 Mbps for unicast. For multicast traffic sent from the access point, all traffic is sent at the base transmission rate, which is usually 24 Mbps or less.

Mobile networks are also challenged by the notion that link connectivity will come and go over time without any effect on a router's interface state. Effectively utilizing a relatively short-lived connection is problematic in IP routed networks, as IP routing protocols tend to rely on interface state and independent timers to maintain convergence, such as HELLO messages or recognition of DEAD routing adjacencies. These dynamic connections can be better utilized with an event-driven paradigm, where acquisition of a new neighbour, or loss of an existing one, is signalled, as opposed to a paradigm driven by timers and interface state. DLEP implements such an event-driven paradigm over a local one-hop TCP session, which guarantees delivery of the event messages.

Another complicating factor for mobile networks is the different methods of physically connecting the modem devices to the router. Modems can be deployed as an interface card in a router's chassis, or as a standalone device connected to the router via Ethernet or serial link. With Ethernet attachment, routing software cannot be aware of convergence events occurring on the radio link, such as acquisition or loss of a potential routing neighbour, nor can the router be aware of the actual capacity of the link. This lack of awareness, along with the variability in data rate, leads to a situation where finding the current best route through the network to a given node is difficult to establish and properly maintain. This is especially true of demand-based access schemes such as Demand Assigned Multiple Access used on some satellite systems, where additional data rate may be available but will not be used unless the network devices emit traffic at a rate higher than the currently established rate. Increasing the traffic rate does not guarantee that additional data rate will be allocated; rather, it may result in data loss and additional retransmissions on the link.

DLEP runs between a router and its attached modem devices, allowing the modem devices to communicate link characteristics as they change, and convergence events, that is the acquisition and loss of potential routing next hops. When the local modem detects the presence of a remote node it sends a message to its router over DLEP. The message consists of an indication of what change has occurred on the link, along with a collection of DLEP-defined Data Items that further describe the change. On receipt, the local router may take whatever action it deems appropriate, such as initiating discovery protocols or issuing HELLO messages to converge the network. On a continuing, as-needed basis, the modem devices use DLEP to report any characteristics of the link that have changed. DLEP is independent of the link type and topology supported by the modem, and is specified to run only on the local link between router and modem. Over-the-air signalling between the local and remote modem may be necessary to provide some parameters, but DLEP does not specify how it is carried out.
sections.plainLanguage: Wireless and satellite links change speed and quality constantly, and sometimes the far end disappears for a while without the router's interface noticing. Routing protocols usually react to that by waiting for timers. DLEP replaces the waiting with an explicit message from the modem: the far end is here, or it is gone, and the link is now this fast.

sections.title: Protocol Overview
sections.content:
DLEP defines a set of Messages used by modems and their attached routers to communicate events that occur on the physical links managed by the modem, for example a remote node entering or leaving the network, or that the link has changed. Associated with these Messages are a set of Data Items, which are pieces of information describing the remote node, such as address information, and the characteristics of the link to the remote node. The modem and router taking part in a session are called DLEP Participants.

DLEP uses a session-oriented paradigm between the modem device and its associated router. If multiple modem devices are attached to a router, or the modem supports multiple connections through multiple logical or physical interfaces, then separate DLEP sessions exist for each modem or connection. A router and modem form a session by completing the discovery and initialization process. The session persists unless or until it either times out, based on the absence of DLEP traffic including heartbeats, or is explicitly torn down by one of the DLEP participants.

The session provides a carrier for information exchange concerning destinations that are available via the modem device. Destinations can be identified by either the router or the modem, and represent a specific, addressable location that can be reached via the links managed by the modem. The Messages concerning destinations become the way for routers and modems to maintain and notify each other about an information base representing the physical and logical destinations accessible via the modem, and the link characteristics to those destinations.

A destination can be either physical or logical. The example of a physical destination is a remote, far-end router attached via the variable-quality network. For physical destinations the Media Access Control address is the address of the far-end router, not the modem. The example of a logical destination is multicast. Multicast traffic is handled in IP networks by deriving a Layer 2 MAC address based on the Layer 3 address, so multicast traffic is supported in DLEP simply by treating the derived MAC address as any other destination. To support logical destinations, one of the participants, typically the router, informs the other as to the existence of the logical destination, and the modem then reports link characteristics for it just as for any other destination. The specific algorithms a modem uses to derive metrics on logical destinations are outside the scope of the specification.

Extensions to DLEP will in all likelihood be necessary as more link types are used. Such extensions are additional Messages, Data Items and status codes with associated rules of behaviour that are not defined in the document. DLEP contains a standard mechanism for router and modem implementations to negotiate the available extensions to use on a per-session basis.
sections.plainLanguage: A DLEP session is between one router and one modem connection. Everything exchanged on it is about destinations, the addressable places reachable through the modem, either a real far-end router or a logical one such as a multicast group. Each destination comes with measurements of the link to it.

sections.title: Requirements
sections.content:
DLEP must be implemented on a single Layer 2 domain. The protocol identifies next-hop destinations by using the MAC address for delivering data traffic, and no manipulation or substitution is performed: the MAC address supplied in all DLEP Messages is used as the Destination MAC address for frames emitted by the participating router. MAC addresses must be unique within the context of the router-modem session.

To enforce the single Layer 2 domain, implementations must support the Generalized TTL Security Mechanism of RFC 5082, and must adhere to the specification for all DLEP Messages. DLEP specifies UDP multicast for single-hop discovery signalling and TCP for transport of the Messages. Modems and routers participating in DLEP sessions must have topologically consistent IP addresses assigned, and it is recommended that implementations use IPv6 link-local addresses to reduce the administrative burden of address assignment. DLEP relies on the guaranteed delivery of its Messages between router and modem once the one-hop discovery process is complete, hence the specification of TCP to carry the Messages. Other reliable transports are possible but outside the scope of the document.

IANA has assigned the port number 854 for DLEP, valid for both TCP and UDP, the IPv4 multicast address 224.0.0.117 for DLEP Discovery, and the IPv6 multicast address FF02:0:0:0:0:0:1:7 for the same purpose.

Two deployment styles are described. A dedicated deployment has the DLEP routers and modems either directly connected or connected to a dedicated switch, for example a router with a line-of-sight radio in one interface and a satellite modem in another. In mobile environments the router and the connected modem or modems are placed into a mobile platform such as a vehicle, boat, or airplane. The resulting network segment is constrained to a small number of devices and is not generally accessible from anywhere else in the network. A networked deployment places the DLEP router and modem on a segment accessible from other points in the network, and the router and a given modem may be multiple physical hops apart, which requires Layer 2 tunnelling to enforce the single-hop requirement.

The specification assumes that a signalling protocol exists between modems participating in a network, carrying or yielding information such as the arrival and departure of modems from the network and the variation of link characteristics between them. It also assumes that the link between router and modem is static with respect to data rate and latency, and that this link is not likely to be the cause of a performance bottleneck. In deployments where the router and modem are separated by multiple network hops, DLEP statistics on the radio links could be insufficient for routing protocols to make appropriate routing decisions, especially when the Layer 2 tunnel is itself served in part or in total by a wireless backhaul link.
sections.plainLanguage: DLEP is a one-hop protocol: the router and the modem must sit on the same Layer 2 network, and the one-hop rule is enforced by requiring the TTL of every packet to be exactly 255. Discovery uses multicast over UDP, and everything after that uses TCP, so messages cannot be lost. IPv6 link-local addresses are recommended so that no address plan is needed.

sections.title: DLEP Session Flow
sections.content:
All DLEP participants of a session move through a number of distinct states: Peer Discovery, Session Initialization, In-Session, Session Termination and Session Reset. Modems, and routers supporting DLEP discovery, transition through all five. Routers that rely on preconfigured TCP address and port information start in the Session Initialization state. Modems must support the Peer Discovery state.

In the Peer Discovery state, routers that support DLEP discovery must send Peer Discovery Signals to initiate modem discovery, and then wait for a Peer Offer Signal response. While in this state, Peer Discovery Signals must be sent repeatedly at regular intervals. It is recommended that this interval be 60 seconds; the interval must be a minimum of 1 second and should be a configurable parameter. This operation is outside the DLEP transaction model, which only describes Messages on a TCP session. A router receiving a Peer Offer Signal must use one of the modem address and port combinations from it to establish a TCP connection, even if a priori configuration exists. If multiple Connection Point Data Items exist, routers should prioritize IPv6 connection points over IPv4 ones. If a TCP connection cannot be achieved using any of the address and port combinations, the router should resume issuing Peer Discovery Signals. In this state the modem must listen for incoming Peer Discovery Signals on the DLEP well-known IPv6 and/or IPv4 link-local multicast address and port, and on receipt of a valid signal must reply with a Peer Offer Signal.

On establishment of the TCP connection, and of the TLS session if TLS is in use, both modem and router enter the Session Initialization state. The router must send a Session Initialization Message and then wait for a Session Initialization Response Message. A response containing a Status Data Item with status code 0, Success, indicates that the modem has received and processed the message, and the router must transition to the In-Session state. The modem must wait for a Session Initialization Message, and on receipt must send a Session Initialization Response Message, and the session transitions to the In-Session state. If the modem receives any other Message, or fails to parse the received Message, it must not send any Message, must terminate the TCP connection and transition to the Session Reset state. Extension negotiation happens here: extensions supported by an implementation must be declared with the Extensions Supported Data Item, and once both participants have exchanged initialization messages, an implementation must not emit any Message, Signal, Data Item, or status code associated with an extension that was not specified in the received initialization message from its peer.

In the In-Session state, Messages can flow in both directions, indicating changes to the session state, the arrival or departure of reachable destinations, or changes in the state of the links to the destinations. The state is maintained until one participant terminates the session with a Session Termination Message, or its peer does so, after which the implementation transitions to the Session Termination state.

Heartbeats. To maintain the In-Session state, periodic Heartbeat Messages must be exchanged between router and modem, intended to keep the session alive and verify bidirectional connectivity. It is recommended that the interval be 60 seconds; the interval must be a minimum of 1 second and should be configurable. Receipt of any valid DLEP Message resets the heartbeat interval timer, so valid messages take the place of additional heartbeats. An implementation must allow a minimum of two heartbeat intervals to expire with no messages from its peer before terminating the session, sending a Session Termination Message with status code 132, Timed Out.

In the Session Termination state, an implementation that sent a Session Termination Message because of an invalid message or error must wait for a Session Termination Response Message from its peer. A sender should allow four heartbeat intervals to expire before assuming its peer is unresponsive, and any other message received while waiting must be silently ignored. When the sender receives the response or times out, it must transition to the Session Reset state. An implementation that receives a Session Termination Message from its peer enters the Session Termination state, must immediately send a Session Termination Response and transition to the Session Reset state.

In the Session Reset state, the implementation must release all resources allocated for the session, eliminate all destinations in the information base represented by the session, and terminate the TCP connection. Having completed these actions it should return to the relevant initial state: Peer Discovery for modems, and either Peer Discovery or Session Initialization for routers, depending on configuration. If the TCP connection is terminated when an implementation is not in the Session Reset state, the implementation must immediately transition to the Session Reset state.
sections.plainLanguage: A session has five states. The router looks for a modem, opens a TCP connection, and the two exchange opening messages. Then both keep the session alive with periodic heartbeat messages and swap news about destinations and link quality. Either side can end the session, and the last state tears down the connection and forgets what was learned.

sections.title: Signal and Message Structure
sections.content:
DLEP defines two protocol units used in two different ways. Signals are only used in the Discovery mechanism and are carried in UDP datagrams. Messages are used bidirectionally over a TCP connection between the participants, in the Session Initialization, In-Session and Session Termination states.

Both Signals and Messages consist of a Header followed by an unordered list of Data Items. Headers consist of Type and Length information, while Data Items are encoded as TLV, type-length-value, structures. There is no restriction on the order of Data Items following a Header, and the acceptability of duplicate Data Items is defined by the definition of the Signal or Message declared by the type in the Header. All integers in Header fields and values must be in network byte order.

The DLEP Signal Header contains a 32-bit magic value made of the characters D, L, E and P, which every Signal must start with, then a 16-bit unsigned Signal Type, and a 16-bit unsigned Length giving the length in octets of all of the DLEP Data Items contained in the Signal. That length must not include the length of the Signal Header itself. The Signal Header is immediately followed by zero or more DLEP Data Items, encoded in TLVs.

The DLEP Message Header contains a 16-bit unsigned Message Type and a 16-bit unsigned Length with the same meaning as in the Signal Header. It is immediately followed by zero or more DLEP Data Items.

Every DLEP Data Item has a 16-bit unsigned Data Item Type, a 16-bit unsigned Length giving the length in octets of the Value field, and a Value field of that many octets holding data specific to that Data Item. The Length does not include the Data Item Type and Length fields themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: Every DLEP packet starts with a small header and then a list of items. A signal header carries the four letters DLEP, a signal type and a length. A message header carries a message type and a length. Each item carries its own type, its own length, and the value.

sections.title: Signals and Messages
sections.content:
Processing rules. If an unrecognized or unexpected Signal is received, or if a received Signal contains unrecognized, invalid, or disallowed duplicate Data Items, the receiving implementation must ignore the Signal. A Signal received with a TTL value that is not equal to 255 must also be ignored. If an unrecognized Message is received, the implementation must issue a Session Termination Message with status code 128, Unknown Message, and transition to the Session Termination state. An unexpected Message leads to status code 129, Unexpected Message. A Message containing unrecognized, invalid, or disallowed duplicate Data Items leads to status code 130, Invalid Data. A packet in the TCP stream received with a TTL value other than 255 makes the receiver immediately transition to the Session Reset state.

No Messages concerning a destination may be sent before the exchange of Destination Up and Destination Up Response, or Destination Announce and Destination Announce Response. A Message about an unannounced destination makes the receiver terminate the session with status code 131, Invalid Destination. After exchanging Destination Down and Destination Down Response, no Messages concerning that destination may be sent until a new Destination Up or Destination Announce is sent.

Status codes. The behaviour of a participant receiving a Message containing a Status Data Item is defined by the failure mode associated with the status code. All status code values less than 100 have a failure mode of Continue, and all other status codes have a failure mode of Terminate. A participant receiving any Message apart from a Session Termination Message that contains a Status Data Item with a Terminate failure mode must immediately issue a Session Termination Message echoing the received Status Data Item and transition to the Session Termination state. A Continue failure mode means normal operation of the session can carry on.

The registered Message types run from 1 to 16: Session Initialization, Session Initialization Response, Session Update, Session Update Response, Session Termination, Session Termination Response, Destination Up, Destination Up Response, Destination Announce, Destination Announce Response, Destination Down, Destination Down Response, Destination Update, Link Characteristics Request, Link Characteristics Response, and Heartbeat. The two Signals are Peer Discovery, type 1, and Peer Offer, type 2. The Peer Discovery Signal is sent by a router to discover modems, in a UDP packet whose destination is the DLEP well-known address and port, with the source IP address set to the router IP address associated with the DLEP interface. The Peer Offer Signal is the modem's response, in a UDP packet whose IP source and destination fields are the swapped values of the Peer Discovery Signal. It may carry IPv4 and IPv6 Connection Point Data Items, which tell the router which unicast address to use when connecting the DLEP TCP session.

The Session Initialization Message is the first Message of the TCP session. It must contain one Heartbeat Interval Data Item and one Peer Type Data Item, and, if DLEP extensions are supported, an Extensions Supported Data Item. It may also carry IPv4 and IPv6 Address Data Items and IPv4 and IPv6 Attached Subnet Data Items. The Session Initialization Response Message must contain a Status, a Peer Type, a Heartbeat Interval, and the data rate and latency metrics, and must contain the Resources, Relative Link Quality and MTU Data Items if those will be used during the session. It also declares every metric the modem will report, with default values, so the modem is announcing which metrics it supports; receipt of a later message with a metric that was not declared is an error that terminates the session. Heartbeats do not start until the response arrives, so implementations must use their own timeout heuristics for that message.

Extensions. Extensions must be negotiated on a per-session basis during session initialization through the Extensions Supported mechanism, and implementations are not required to support any extension to be DLEP compliant. Interoperable extensions need to be standardized either as an update to the document or as a standalone specification, and the IANA registries contain sufficient unassigned space for Signals, Messages, Data Items, and status codes to accommodate future extensions. The document registers Private Use numbering space in the Signal, Message, Data Item and status code registries for experimental extensions, called experiments, whose use must be announced as DLEP extensions with an identifier agreed between the participants. Using several experiments in one session is discouraged, because clashes of experimental definitions could lead to interoperability issues.

Scalability. The protocol is intended to support thousands of destinations on a given modem and router pair. On a large scale an implementation should consider techniques to prevent flooding its peer with a large number of Messages in a short time, for example a dampening algorithm to stop a flapping device from generating many Destination Up and Destination Down Messages. Hysteresis can lessen the impact of rapid, minor fluctuations in link quality. The specific algorithms are outside the scope of the specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The two discovery signals are sent over UDP and are simply ignored when they are not understood. The sixteen message types travel over TCP. A message that is unknown, unexpected or malformed ends the session with a status code that says why. Status codes below 100 mean the session carries on; the rest end it. Before a destination can be talked about, it must have been announced.

sections.title: DLEP Data Items
sections.content:
The registered Data Item types run from 1 to 20: Status, IPv4 Connection Point, IPv6 Connection Point, Peer Type, Heartbeat Interval, Extensions Supported, MAC Address, IPv4 Address, IPv6 Address, IPv4 Attached Subnet, IPv6 Attached Subnet, Maximum Data Rate for receive and transmit, Current Data Rate for receive and transmit, Latency, Resources, Relative Link Quality for receive and transmit, and Maximum Transmission Unit. The Status Data Item carries a one-octet Status Code and an optional UTF-8 Text field describing the cause; if no Text is supplied the Length field must be set to 1.

DLEP includes the ability for the router and modem to communicate metrics that reflect the characteristics of the variable-quality link in use. DLEP does not specify how a given metric value is calculated; the protocol assumes that metrics have been calculated on a best-effort basis, incorporating all pertinent data available to the modem device. Metrics based on large-enough sample sizes will preclude short traffic bursts from adversely skewing reported values.

Metrics can be sent in two contexts: for a specific destination within the network, and per session, meaning those that apply to all destinations accessed via the modem. Most metrics can be further subdivided into transmit and receive metrics. Where metrics are provided at the session level, the router propagates them to all entries in its information base for destinations accessed via the modem. Modems announce all metric Data Items that will be reported during the session and provide default values for them in the Session Initialization Response Message, and to use a metric type that was not included there the modem terminates the session and establishes a new one.

A modem can send metrics both in a session context, through the Session Update Message, and in a specific destination context, through the Destination Update Message, at any time. The most recently received metric value takes precedence over any earlier value, regardless of context: metrics received in a destination context update that destination, while metrics received in a session-wide context update the metrics for all destinations accessed via the modem. It is left to implementations to choose sensible default values. Modems with static link metric characteristics can report metrics only once for a given destination, or once on a session-wide basis.

In addition to communicating existing metrics about the link, DLEP provides a Message allowing a router to request a different data rate or latency from the modem. The Link Characteristics Request Message gives the router the ability to deal with requisite increases or decreases of allocated data rate and latency in demand-based schemes in a more deterministic manner.
sections.plainLanguage: The data items are the actual content: addresses, the MAC address of a destination, the data rate the link can currently carry in each direction, its latency, its quality, and its maximum transmission unit. Metrics can be reported for the whole session or for one destination, and the newer value always wins. The modem also has to say up front which metrics it will report during the session.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The potential security concerns when using DLEP are as follows. An attacker might pretend to be a DLEP participant, either at session initialization or by injection of DLEP Messages once a session has been established. DLEP Data Items could be altered by an attacker, causing the receiving implementation to inappropriately alter its information base concerning network status. An attacker could join an unsecured radio network and inject over-the-air signals that maliciously influence the information reported by a DLEP modem, causing a router to forward traffic to an inappropriate destination.

The implications of attacks on DLEP peers are directly proportional to the extent to which DLEP data is used within the control plane. While the use of DLEP data in other control-plane components is out of scope, as an example, if DLEP statistics are incorporated into route cost calculations, adversaries masquerading as a DLEP peer and injecting malicious data could cause suboptimal route selection, adversely impacting network performance. Similar issues arise if DLEP data is used as an input to policing algorithms, where injection of malicious data could cause incorrect decisions and degrade network throughput.

For these reasons, security of the DLEP transport must be considered at both the transport layer and Layer 2. At the transport layer, when TLS is in use, each peer should check the validity of credentials presented by the other peer during TLS session establishment. Implementations following the dedicated deployment model attempting to use TLS may need to consider pre-shared keys, specialized techniques for peer identity validation, and RFC 5487. Implementations following the networked deployment model should refer to BCP 195, RFC 7525.

At Layer 2, since DLEP is restricted to operation over a single, possibly logical, hop, implementations should also secure the Layer 2 link, for example with IEEE 802.1AE or IEEE 802.1X. By examining the Secured Medium flag in the Peer Type Data Item, a router can decide if it is able to trust the information supplied via a DLEP modem. If it is not, the router should consider restricting the size of attached subnets announced in the IPv4 and IPv6 Attached Subnet Data Items that are considered for route selection.

To avoid potential denial-of-service attacks, it is recommended that implementations using the Peer Discovery mechanism maintain an information base of hosts that persistently fail Session Initialization, even though those hosts have provided an acceptable Peer Discovery Signal, and ignore any subsequent Peer Discovery Signals from such hosts. The specification does not address security of the data plane, as it is not affected, and standard security procedures can be employed.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone who can talk to the modem can lie about the link, and a router that believes the lie sends traffic the wrong way. So the session should be protected with TLS, and the Layer 2 link beneath it should be secured as well. A router can also look at the Secured Medium flag to decide how much to trust a modem that is on an open network.
